title: Does a boutique R&D tax advisor sign the tax return as a paid preparer?
description: A boutique R&D tax advisor generally does not sign a client's original return as paid preparer but can face IRC § 6694 penalties as a nonsigning preparer.
summary: Under U.S. federal tax law, a boutique R&D tax advisor generally does not sign a client's original income tax return as the paid preparer; the CPA or tax officer primarily responsible for the overall return signs. Boutique advisors sign only standalone amended returns or refund claims they prepare, yet can still face IRC § 6694 penalties as nonsigning preparers.

body.text: Under U.S. federal tax law, a boutique R&D tax advisor generally does not sign a client's original income tax return as the paid preparer; the CPA or tax officer primarily responsible for the overall return signs. Boutique advisors sign only standalone amended returns or refund claims they prepare, yet can still face IRC § 6694 penalties as nonsigning preparers.

Under the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) and Treasury Regulations currently in force in the United States, a boutique research and development (R&D) tax advisor generally does not sign a taxpayer's original federal income tax return as a "paid preparer". Pursuant to 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.6695-1(b)(1) (promulgated by Treasury Decision 9436, 73 FR 78430, effective December 22, 2008, and applicable to returns and claims for refund filed, and advice provided, after December 31, 2008), only the single individual signing tax return preparer—defined as the individual tax return preparer who bears primary responsibility for the overall substantive accuracy of the preparation of the entire return or claim for refund—is legally required and permitted to sign the "Paid Preparer Use Only" block. When a boutique R&D specialist is engaged alongside a taxpayer's general Certified Public Accountant (CPA) firm or internal corporate tax department to conduct a Research Credit Study under 26 U.S.C. § 41 and compute the figures for Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities), two structural rules govern signature responsibility: first, Form 6765 is an informational and computational attachment that contains no jurat, taxpayer signature block, or "Paid Preparer Use Only" section of its own (Form 6765, Rev. December 2024; Instructions for Form 6765, Rev. December 2025 for use with the January 2025 revision, posted February 6, 2026, and updated April 30, 2026); second, the external CPA or corporate tax officer who assembles, reviews, and files the complete income tax return (such as Form 1120, Form 1120-S, Form 1065, or Form 1040) retains primary responsibility for the overall substantive accuracy of the return. A boutique R&D advisor becomes a signing tax return preparer only when the boutique firm itself prepares and presents for filing a standalone amended return or claim for refund (such as Form 1120-X, Form 1040-X, or Form 941-X/943-X) whose overarching substantive purpose is the R&D credit claim itself.

Practitioner Analysis — The Nonsigning Preparer Liability Trap: The absence of a signature line on Form 6765 creates a pervasive compliance misconception in specialized tax practice. Boutique R&D advisors frequently assume that because they do not sign the return or enter a Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN) on the filing, they act merely as "consultants" or providers of "mechanical assistance" outside the reach of Internal Revenue Service (IRS) preparer penalties. That assumption is contradicted by the governing statute and regulations. Under 26 U.S.C. § 7701(a)(36)(A) and 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(2)–(3), any advisor who for compensation provides post-event tax advice or prepares a schedule that constitutes a "substantial portion" of a return—defined by a regulatory de minimis safe harbor that is breached whenever the Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) on which the credit is determined equal or exceed $400,000, or equal or exceed $10,000 while also equaling or exceeding 20 percent of the taxpayer's gross income (or adjusted gross income for an individual)—is legally classified as a nonsigning tax return preparer. Furthermore, under the cross-firm liability rule of 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(b)(1) and (b)(6) Example 4, where a nonsigning boutique R&D advisor and a signing CPA belong to different firms, the IRS is not limited to penalizing one individual per return: both the boutique R&D advisor and the signing CPA can be found primarily responsible and simultaneously assessed understatement penalties under 26 U.S.C. § 6694(a) (the greater of $1,000 or 50 percent of each preparer's respective fee) or § 6694(b) (the greater of $5,000 or 75 percent of each preparer's respective fee).
1. The Mechanics of Form 6765 and the Single Signing Preparer Rule
1.1 How Form 6765 Connects to Federal Tax Returns

To claim the federal credit for increasing research activities under 26 U.S.C. § 41, make the reduced credit election under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c), or elect the qualified small business payroll tax credit under 26 U.S.C. § 41(h), a taxpayer must complete and attach Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, OMB No. 1545-0619, Attachment Sequence No. 676; Form PDF Rev. December 2024; Instructions for Form 6765 Rev. December 2025 for use with the January 2025 revision, posted February 6, 2026, updated April 30, 2026, and supplemented by the June 18, 2025 controlled-group clarification updated June 28, 2026). Under the official IRS Instructions for Form 6765, Form 6765 is never filed as a standalone tax return; rather, it is an attachment to the taxpayer's primary federal income tax return—such as Form 1120 (U.S. Corporation Income Tax Return for C corporations), Form 1120-S (U.S. Income Tax Return for an S Corporation), Form 1065 (U.S. Return of Partnership Income), Form 1040 (U.S. Individual Income Tax Return), or Form 1041 (U.S. Income Tax Return for Estates and Trusts)—or to an amended return or administrative adjustment request (AAR).

For taxpayers other than partnerships and S corporations, the current-year research credit computed in Section C of Form 6765 (Line 30, or Line 32 for estates and trusts after beneficiary allocations on Line 31) flows onto Form 3800 (General Business Credit, Part III)—specifically onto Part III, Line 4i for eligible small businesses or Part III, Line 1c for all other filers—before reducing income tax liability on the main return. Partnerships and S corporations do not file Form 3800 to claim the research credit; instead, they must file Form 6765 with their entity return and report the credit (reduced by any Section D payroll tax credit election on Line 36) on Schedule K, distributing each partner's or shareholder's allocable share on Schedule K-1 (Form 1065, Box 15, Code M for partnerships; Form 1120-S, Box 13, Code M for S corporations; and Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), Box 13, Code I for estates and trusts). Where a qualified small business (QSB) elects under Section D of Form 6765 (Lines 33a through 36) to apply up to $500,000 of its research credit against the employer portion of Social Security (and Medicare) payroll tax liabilities, the taxpayer must also complete and attach Form 8974 (Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Credit for Increasing Research Activities, carrying the Line 36 amount to Form 8974, Part 1, column (e)) to its quarterly or annual employment tax return—Form 941 (Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return), Form 941 (PR), Form 941-SS, Form 943 (Employer's Annual Federal Tax Return for Agricultural Employees), or Form 944 (Employer's Annual Federal Tax Return)—or to an adjusted employment tax return or claim for refund (Form 941-X or Form 943-X).

Crucially, an inspection of Form 6765 (Pages 1 through 3, covering Header Questions A and B and Sections A through G) confirms that Form 6765 does not contain a jurat, a taxpayer signature line, or a "Paid Preparer Use Only" signature block. Instead, the official taxpayer jurat and the "Paid Preparer Use Only" section—containing fields for the preparer's printed name, preparer's signature, date, PTIN, firm's name, firm's Employer Identification Number (EIN), firm's address, phone number, and self-employed checkbox—appear exclusively on the primary tax return (Form 1120, Form 1120-S, Form 1065, Form 1040, Form 1041, Form 941, Form 943, Form 944) or on the formal amended return, claim for refund, or AAR (Form 1120-X, Form 1040-X, Form 941-X, Form 943-X, Form 8082, or Form 8985). When a taxpayer electronically files its return and includes a third-party research credit study or supporting statements, the December 2025 Instructions for Form 6765 require the electronic PDF attachments to be transmitted as named files within the e-file submission package—specifically Form6765Study.pdf for credit studies, Form6765ClaimInformation.pdf for amended return claim information, Form6765ItemASection280C.pdf for Section 280C election statements, Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf for statistical sampling plans, and Form6765ASC730AppendixA.pdf through Form6765ASC730AppendixD.pdf for ASC 730 Directive filings—all under the single electronic signature of the primary return's signing preparer on Form 8879 (IRS e-file Signature Authorization).

Under 26 U.S.C. § 6695(b) and 26 CFR § 1.6695-1(b)(1) (promulgated by T.D. 9436, 73 FR 78430, Dec. 22, 2008, as corrected by 74 FR 5104, Jan. 29, 2009, and Announcement 2009-15, 2009-11 I.R.B.), the legal obligation to sign a return or claim for refund applies solely to an individual who is a signing tax return preparer within the meaning of 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(1). Section 301.7701-15(b)(1) defines a signing tax return preparer in exact regulatory terms:
"A signing tax return preparer is the individual tax return preparer who has the primary responsibility for the overall substantive accuracy of the preparation of such return or claim for refund."

Under 26 CFR § 1.6695-1(b)(1), for a non-electronically signed return, the signing tax return preparer must manually sign the return or claim for refund after it is completed and before it is presented to the taxpayer (or nontaxable entity) for signature. If the primary signing preparer is physically unavailable to sign (for example, out of town for a week on another assignment, as in 26 CFR § 1.6695-1(b)(4) Example 4, rather than merely detailed to another office in the same city for the day), another tax return preparer within the firm must review the entire preparation of the return or claim for refund, including the information obtained relative to the taxpayer, and then sign it. Furthermore, IRS administrative guidance in Frequently Asked Questions: Do I Need a PTIN? (last updated October 9, 2026) explicitly confirms that the PTIN registration rules do not alter who is designated as the signing tax return preparer under 26 CFR §§ 1.6695-1(b) and 301.7701-15(b)(1). Only the single signing tax return preparer who bears primary responsibility for the overall substantive accuracy of the return signs the "Paid Preparer Use Only" block and furnishes their PTIN under 26 CFR § 1.6109-2(a). Non-signing preparers do not sign the return, their names and PTINs are not disclosed on the tax return, and the IRS has explicitly confirmed that "there is no plan to expand the paid preparer section of tax returns to include non-signing preparers".
1.2 Practitioner Analysis: Distinguishing Original Returns from Standalone Refund Claims

Because signing status turns on which individual practitioner holds primary responsibility for the overall substantive accuracy of the filed tax document under 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.6695-1(b)(4) Examples 1 through 4, a boutique R&D tax advisor's obligation to sign depends directly on the procedural vehicle through which the IRC § 41 credit is claimed.

When a company engages a boutique R&D advisory firm to perform an engineering and financial study for an original income tax return (Form 1120, Form 1120-S, Form 1065, or Form 1040) that is prepared and filed by the company's external CPA firm, the boutique advisor is only preparing a single credit schedule (Form 6765, along with Section E/F summaries, Section G business component schedules, and Item A Section 280C or Item B controlled-group attachments) within a comprehensive income tax return that reports total gross receipts, cost of goods sold, depreciation, domestic research deductions or amortization under IRC § 174A, officer compensation, state tax deductions, international inclusions, and overall tax liability. The general CPA firm reviews and integrates the Form 6765 outputs into Form 3800 (or Schedule K / K-1) and the main return. Under 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(1) and § 1.6695-1(b)(4) Example 2 (where national accounting firm partner K conducts the final review and makes final determinations of tax liability on client H's return), the partner or principal at the general CPA firm holds primary responsibility for the overall substantive accuracy of the income tax return and must sign as the paid preparer. The boutique R&D advisor cannot and does not sign the original return as the paid preparer, and instead occupies the legal status of a nonsigning tax return preparer under 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(2) (assuming the study exceeds the de minimis safe harbor thresholds analyzed in Section 2).

Similarly, if a large corporation's internal tax department prepares and files its own original Form 1120 using employees who are regularly and continuously employed by the corporation, those internal employees are statutorily excluded from the definition of a "tax return preparer" under 26 U.S.C. § 7701(a)(36)(B)(ii) and 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(f)(1)(ix) (which also covers employees of a parent or subsidiary corporation owning more than 50 percent of the voting power of the taxpayer under § 301.7701-15(f)(1)(ix)). Even though no external CPA signs the "Paid Preparer Use Only" block on that self-prepared corporate Form 1120, an external boutique R&D advisor who only prepared the Form 6765 R&D credit study still did not assume primary responsibility for the overall substantive accuracy of the corporation's entire Form 1120. Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(b)(3) and (b)(6) Example 3 and § 1.6694-2(d)(3)(v) Example 2 explicitly address this exact configuration: where neither the specialist advisor nor anyone in the specialist's firm signs the corporate taxpayer's return because the specialist only advised on or prepared specific complex entries constituting a substantial portion of the return, there is no signing tax return preparer for that return, and the boutique R&D specialist is regulated as a nonsigning tax return preparer.

Conversely, as documented in the IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG, May 2008), boutique R&D consultants frequently prepare and present to the taxpayer the formal amended return or claim for refund (such as Form 1120-X or Form 1040-X) when a retroactive R&D study is conducted for prior open tax years. When the sole substantive adjustment on Form 1120-X is the retroactive claim of the IRC § 41 research credit, and the boutique R&D advisor drafts the Form 1120-X (relying in good faith without verification on the previously filed original return's baseline figures as permitted by 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(e)(2)), prepares the attached Form 6765, compiles the mandatory Five Items of Information for amended research credit claims, and presents the completed Form 1120-X to the client for signature, the boutique R&D advisor holds primary responsibility for the overall substantive accuracy of that claim for refund. In that scenario, the individual lead practitioner at the boutique R&D firm is a signing tax return preparer under 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(1) and must sign the "Paid Preparer Use Only" block on the Form 1120-X (and furnish their PTIN and the boutique firm's EIN) to avoid penalties under 26 U.S.C. § 6695(b) and (c). If, however, the boutique R&D firm merely delivers the retroactive study and Form 6765 schedules to the taxpayer's general CPA firm, and the general CPA firm prepares, reviews, and files the Form 1120-X (or, for a partnership subject to the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 [BBA], files an Administrative Adjustment Request using Forms 8082, 8985, and 8986), then the general CPA signs the amended return or AAR as the signing preparer and the boutique R&D advisor remains a nonsigning preparer.

body.text: 2. Statutory and Regulatory Classification: When Is a Boutique R&D Advisor a Tax Return Preparer?
2.1 The Statutory Definition and the Mechanical Assistance Trap

Under 26 U.S.C. § 7701(a)(36)(A) (as amended by Section 8246 of the Small Business and Work Opportunity Tax Act of 2007, Pub. L. 110-28, 121 Stat. 201, effective for returns prepared after May 25, 2007, which broadened the statute from "income tax return preparer" to all federal tax returns and refund claims under Title 26), the term tax return preparer is defined broadly:

"The term 'tax return preparer' means any person who prepares for compensation, or who employs one or more persons to prepare for compensation, any return of tax imposed by this title or any claim for refund of tax imposed by this title. For purposes of the preceding sentence, the preparation of a substantial portion of a return or claim for refund shall be treated as if it were the preparation of such return or claim for refund."

Three foundational provisions in 26 CFR § 301.7701-15 (applicable to returns and claims for refund filed, and advice provided, after December 31, 2008 per § 301.7701-15(g)) eliminate the standard defenses raised by non-CPA R&D consulting firms. First, under 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(d) (Qualifications), "[a] person may be a tax return preparer without regard to educational qualifications and professional status requirements." Whether a boutique R&D firm's study is conducted by software engineers, metallurgists, PhD chemists, uncredentialed tax consultants, attorneys, Enrolled Agents, or CPAs, their lack of a CPA license or formal enrollment to practice before the IRS has no bearing on their legal classification as a tax return preparer. In Goulding v. United States, 957 F.2d 1420 (7th Cir. 1992), and Wilfong v. United States, 991 F.2d 359, 366 n.10 (7th Cir. 1993), the Seventh Circuit confirmed that the statutory preparer regime and its negligence and understatement standards apply equally across licensed professionals and non-CPA preparers alike.

Second, while 26 U.S.C. § 7701(a)(36)(B)(i) and 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(f)(1)(viii) exclude a person who furnishes only "typing, reproduction, or other mechanical assistance in the preparation of a return or claim for refund," 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(c) (Mechanical or clerical assistance) establishes the converse rule that directly captures boutique R&D studies:

"A person who furnishes to a taxpayer or other tax return preparer sufficient information and advice so that completion of the return or claim for refund is largely a mechanical or clerical matter is considered a tax return preparer, even though that person does not actually place or review placement of information on the return or claim for refund."

Furthermore, 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(i) specifies that "[a] person who renders tax advice on a position that is directly relevant to the determination of the existence, characterization, or amount of an entry on a return or claim for refund will be regarded as having prepared that entry." When a boutique R&D advisor evaluates a taxpayer's projects under the four-part test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2), calculates qualified wage, supply, computer rental, and 65 percent (or 75 percent / 100 percent) contract research expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b), and delivers a completed Form 6765 draft or line-by-line QRE schedule so that the external CPA firm merely keys those figures into tax preparation software, the boutique advisor has furnished sufficient information and advice to be treated as the preparer of those entries.

Third, 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(2)(i) defines a nonsigning tax return preparer as any tax return preparer who is not a signing tax return preparer "but who prepares all or a substantial portion of a return or claim for refund within the meaning of paragraph (b)(3) of this section with respect to events that have occurred at the time the advice is rendered." If an advisor renders tax advice solely before a transaction or research activity occurs (prospective tax planning) and provides no post-event advice, the advisor is not a tax return preparer (26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(2)(ii) Example 2)—unless all facts and circumstances show that (1) the position giving rise to an understatement is primarily attributable to the pre-event advice, (2) the advice was given before events occurred primarily to avoid treating the person as a tax return preparer, and (3) the advice was confirmed after events occurred for purposes of preparing a tax return. Moreover, in determining whether an individual is a nonsigning tax return preparer, time spent on advice given after events have occurred that represents less than 5 percent of the aggregate time incurred by that individual with respect to the position(s) giving rise to the understatement is disregarded (26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(2)(i)). Because standard R&D tax credit studies are conducted after the close of the tax year (or during fourth-quarter and post-year-end data collection after the underlying research expenditures have been paid or incurred), virtually 100 percent of a boutique R&D advisor's study hours occur after the relevant events have occurred, easily surpassing the 5 percent post-event time threshold.
2.2 The Substantial Portion Test and the Nonsigning Safe Harbor

Under 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(i), whether a schedule, entry, or other portion of a return or claim for refund constitutes a substantial portion is determined by whether the person knows or reasonably should know that the tax attributable to the schedule, entry, or other portion is a substantial portion of the tax required to be shown on the return or claim for refund. The regulation explicitly states that "[a] single tax entry may constitute a substantial portion of the tax required to be shown on a return." Factors to consider in determining whether a schedule, entry, or other portion is a substantial portion include, but are not limited to: (A) the size and complexity of the item relative to the taxpayer's gross income; and (B) the size of the understatement attributable to the item compared to the taxpayer's reported tax liability.

To provide objective mathematical certainty for nonsigning tax return preparers only—explicitly excluding signing preparers under 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(ii)(C)—26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(ii)(A) establishes a two-tier de minimis safe harbor. A schedule, entry, or other portion of a return or claim for refund is not considered a substantial portion if it involves amounts of gross income, amounts of deductions, or amounts on the basis of which credits are determined that are:

items: Less than $10,000; OR
Less than $400,000 AND also less than 20 percent of the gross income as shown on the return or claim for refund (or, for an individual, the individual's adjusted gross income).

body.text: Under 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(ii)(B), if more than one schedule, entry, or other portion is involved, all schedules, entries, or other portions prepared or advised on by the nonsigning preparer must be aggregated when applying this de minimis safe harbor. (Historical Currency Note: Prior to the promulgation of T.D. 9436 on December 22, 2008, earlier versions of 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(2)—such as the pre-2009 regulations analyzed in Goulding v. United States, 957 F.2d 1420 (7th Cir. 1992), and Mindell v. United States, 693 F. Supp. 847 (C.D. Cal. 1988)—set these de minimis cutoffs at less than $2,000, or less than $100,000 and less than 20 percent of gross income or adjusted gross income; for all returns filed and advice provided after December 31, 2008, the current $10,000 and $400,000 / 20 percent thresholds govern.)
2.3 Worked Hypothetical Examples: Applying the Amounts on the Basis of Which Credits Are Determined Test

Practitioner Analysis — Why QREs (Not Net Credit Dollars) Govern the Safe Harbor: The exact wording of 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(ii)(A) is decisive for R&D tax credit specialists: the $10,000 and $400,000 safe harbor thresholds apply to "amounts on the basis of which credits are determined," not to the final net tax credit dollar figure itself. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1) (the 20 percent regular credit, or 15.8 percent reduced regular credit on Form 6765 Line 13 if the Section 280C election is made) and 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(A)–(B) (the 14 percent or 6 percent Alternative Simplified Credit [ASC] on Form 6765 Line 24, which is multiplied by 79 percent on Line 26 if the Section 280C reduced credit is elected), the research credit is determined on the basis of the taxpayer's Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) reported on Form 6765 Line 48 (plus any basic research payments or energy research consortium payments). Furthermore, if the taxpayer checks "No" on Item A of Form 6765 and does not elect the reduced credit under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c) on its original timely filed return (including extensions), the taxpayer must reduce its domestic research and experimental expenditure deductions (or capitalized and amortized amounts) under 26 U.S.C. § 174A (enacted by Public Law 119-21 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024) by the amount of the research credit, which constitutes an additional deduction adjustment that must be aggregated with the credit basis under 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(ii)(B).

To demonstrate how these thresholds operate mathematically, consider three hypothetical engagements in which a boutique R&D advisory firm conducts a post-year-end study and delivers Form 6765 figures to an external CPA firm that prepares and signs the taxpayer's corporate Form 1120.

In Hypothetical Scenario A (Early-Stage Startup — Below the $10,000 Safe Harbor), Startup Alpha Corp has $150,000 in gross income for Tax Year 2025 and had $0 QREs in the three preceding tax years (2022–2024). Alpha engages Boutique R&D Firm after year-end to evaluate a small prototype project. Boutique R&D Firm determines that Alpha incurred $8,000 in total QREs during 2025 (reported on Form 6765 Section F, Line 48 and Section B, Line 20) and checks "Yes" on Item A to elect the Section 280C(c) reduced credit. Because Alpha had no QREs in any one of the three preceding tax years, Alpha skips Lines 21 through 23 on Form 6765, and under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(B)(ii) and Form 6765 Line 24, its gross ASC rate is 6 percent of current-year QREs, yielding a gross ASC credit of 8,000 × 0.06 = $480.00) on Line 24 and Line 25, and a net Section 280C(c) reduced credit of 480.00 × 0.79 = $379.20) on Line 26. Because the amount on the basis of which the credit is determined (total QREs of $8,000) is less than $10,000, under 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(ii)(A)(1) the Form 6765 schedule is not a substantial portion of Alpha's return. Consequently, Boutique R&D Firm is neither a signing nor a nonsigning tax return preparer under 26 U.S.C. § 7701(a)(36) (though it remains subject to general aiding-and-abetting liability under 26 U.S.C. § 6701 if it knowingly assists in a false understatement).

In Hypothetical Scenario B (Mid-Market Company — Protected by the $400,000 and 20% Gross Income Safe Harbor), Beta Manufacturing Inc. reports $2,500,000 in gross income on its Form 1120, and its average annual QREs for the three preceding tax years were $150,000 (total prior 3-year QREs of $450,000 on Form 6765 Line 21). Boutique R&D Firm conducts a post-year-end study and determines that Beta incurred $250,000 in current-year QREs (Form 6765 Line 48 and Line 20), electing the 14 percent ASC method under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(A) and the Section 280C(c) reduced credit. Step-by-step, 50 percent of the 3-year average prior QREs (computed on Form 6765 Line 22 by dividing Line 21's $450,000 by 6.0) equals 150,000 × 0.50 = $75,000.00); excess current-year QREs on Line 23 equal 250,000 − $75,000 = $175,000.00); multiplying excess QREs by the 14 percent statutory ASC rate on Line 24 produces a 175,000 × 0.14 = $24,500.00); and applying the 79 percent Section 280C(c) multiplier on Line 26 yields a net reduced credit of 24,500.00 × 0.79 = $19,355.00). Meanwhile, 20 percent of Beta's gross income equals 2,500,000 × 0.20 = $500,000.00). Although Beta's $250,000 QRE credit basis exceeds $10,000, it satisfies both prongs of the second safe harbor in 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(ii)(A)(2): $250,000 is less than $400,000, and 500,000.00). Therefore, as a nonsigning advisor, Boutique R&D Firm qualifies for the regulatory de minimis safe harbor and is not deemed to have prepared a "substantial portion" of Beta's Form 1120.

In Hypothetical Scenario C (Commercial R&D Study — Breaching the $400,000 Ceiling Triggers Nonsigning Preparer Status), Gamma Technologies Inc. reports $5,000,000 in gross income on its Form 1120, and its average annual QREs for the three preceding tax years were $300,000 (total prior 3-year QREs of $900,000 on Form 6765 Line 21). Boutique R&D Firm conducts a post-year-end study and determines that Gamma incurred $600,000 in current-year QREs (Form 6765 Line 48 and Line 20). Step-by-step, 50 percent of the 3-year average prior QREs on Line 22 equals 300,000 × 0.50 = $150,000.00, or $900,000 ÷ 6.0); excess current-year QREs on Line 23 equal 600,000 − $150,000 = $450,000.00); and multiplying excess QREs by the 14 percent statutory ASC rate on Line 24 yields a 450,000 × 0.14 = $63,000.00), or 63,000.00 × 0.79 = $49,770.00). Even though Gamma's $600,000 in QREs is less than 20 percent of its 1,000,000.00), the second safe harbor in 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(ii)(A)(2) is conjunctive ("Less than $400,000 and also less than 20 percent of the gross income"). Because $600,000 equals or exceeds $400,000, the safe harbor fails automatically. Given the size and technical complexity of a $600,000 QRE claim generating a 49,770.00 net reduced) tax credit reduction, Boutique R&D Firm has prepared a substantial portion of Gamma's return under 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(i). Gamma's external CPA still signs Form 1120 as the signing tax return preparer, while Boutique R&D Firm (and its lead supervisor on the engagement) is legally classified as a nonsigning tax return preparer subject to full penalty exposure under 26 U.S.C. § 6694.
3. Judicial Precedent on Substantial Portion and Multi-Preparer Returns

Federal courts have consistently upheld Treasury Regulation § 301.7701-15(b) against challenges by non-signing specialists and signing employers alike, establishing four controlling doctrines that directly govern boutique R&D tax advisors.
3.1 Goulding v. United States, 717 F. Supp. 545 (N.D. Ill. 1989), aff'd, 957 F.2d 1420 (7th Cir. 1992), and Wilfong v. United States, 991 F.2d 359 (7th Cir. 1993)

In Goulding v. United States, 957 F.2d 1420 (7th Cir. Mar. 18, 1992) (affirming 717 F. Supp. 545 (N.D. Ill. 1989)), Randall S. Goulding—an attorney, CPA, and former IRS special agent—acted as legal counsel to three research-and-development limited partnerships (Mercon, Ltd., LaSala, Ltd., and Jonquil, Ltd.) that entered into patent purchase agreements to acquire technology rights for $7,000,000 (Mercon), $8,800,000 (LaSala), and $5,302,000 (Jonquil), funded by nominal cash down payments and over $20.75 million in contingent notes alongside research, development, and licensing agreements with National Patent Development Corporation. For his services, the partnerships paid Goulding $90,000 in 1979, $80,000 in 1980, and $86,250 in 1981. Goulding prepared and signed the partnerships' Form 1065 returns, Schedule K, and Schedules K-1, deducting non-deductible start-up costs under IRC § 709 and depreciating the contingent purchase price of unproven patent rights, which flowed through as losses to the individual limited partners' Form 1040 returns. Goulding had no direct contact with the limited partners and never saw, prepared, or signed any of the individual limited partners' Form 1040 returns. Nevertheless, the IRS assessed $53,300 in preparer penalties against Goulding under 26 U.S.C. § 6694(a), deeming him the nonsigning preparer of the individual limited partners' returns under 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3).

The Seventh Circuit unanimously affirmed. Writing for the panel (Circuit Judges Wood, Jr., Flaum, and Ripple), Circuit Judge Ripple held that 26 CFR § 301.7701-15 is a valid, "substantially contemporaneous construction" of the Tax Reform Act of 1976. The court emphasized that under the legislative history (H.R. Rep. No. 658, 94th Cong., 2d Sess. 275), supplying substantive information and advice relating to specific entries on a return makes one a preparer of that return even when someone else fills out and signs the return. Even though Goulding's work boiled down to a single flow-through entry on each partner's Form 1040, that entry reflected a complex financial and legal analysis of R&D partnership expenditures upon which the limited partners and their personal return preparers necessarily relied, constituting a "substantial portion" of the partners' individual returns. Furthermore, the Seventh Circuit explicitly noted the statutory bifurcation between IRC § 6694 (which applies broadly to all preparers of a substantial portion, signing or non-signing) and IRC §§ 6107, 6109, and 6695(a)–(d) (whose signature, PTIN-furnishing, and copy-retention rules are restricted by regulation to signing preparers). One year later, in Wilfong v. United States, 991 F.2d 359, 365–66 (7th Cir. 1993), the Seventh Circuit reaffirmed Goulding, holding that a return preparer bears the burden of proving an absence of negligent disregard of rules or regulations and has an affirmative duty of reasonable inquiry whenever client-supplied information would lead a reasonable, prudent preparer to seek additional corroborating facts.

Practitioner Analysis — Flow-Through R&D Credits on S Corporation and Partnership Returns: Under Goulding and 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(iii), when a boutique R&D advisor prepares a substantial Form 6765 research credit claim for an S corporation (Form 1120-S) or a partnership (Form 1065), the research credit flows directly via Schedule K-1 (Box 13, Code M on Form 1120-S; Box 15, Code M on Form 1065) to the shareholders' or partners' individual Form 1040 returns (via Form 3800 Part III, Line 1c or Line 4i). If that flow-through R&D credit basis exceeds the § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(ii) safe harbor on a shareholder's or partner's Form 1040, the boutique R&D advisor becomes a nonsigning tax return preparer not only of the entity's Form 1120-S or Form 1065, but also of each individual shareholder's or partner's Form 1040, multiplying potential penalty assessments under 26 U.S.C. § 6694 across every investor return.
3.2 Mindell v. United States, 693 F. Supp. 847 (C.D. Cal. 1988)

Arising out of the discovery phase of the Goulding litigation (Randall S. Goulding v. United States, Civ. No. 83 C 5692 (N.D. Ill.)), one of the 83 limited partners, Earl L. Mindell, sued the United States under 26 U.S.C. § 6103, claiming the government unlawfully disclosed his entire personal Form 1040 tax returns, attached schedules, Return Preparer's Checksheet, and Report of Individual Income Tax Changes for the 1979, 1980, and 1981 tax years to Goulding during litigation over whether Goulding had prepared a "substantial portion" of the partners' returns. In Mindell v. United States, 693 F. Supp. 847 (C.D. Cal. May 5, 1988), the district court upheld the validity of 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b) and granted summary judgment to the United States under 26 U.S.C. § 6103(h)(4)(B) and (C). The court held that because determining whether a schedule is a "substantial portion" requires comparing the length, complexity, and tax impact of the prepared schedule against the unprepared portions of the taxpayer's return as a whole, it is impossible to determine whether a third-party specialist is a "tax return preparer" without examining the taxpayer's entire tax return and all accompanying schedules.
3.3 Schneider v. United States, 257 F. Supp. 2d 1154 (S.D. Ind. 2003)

In Schneider v. United States, 257 F. Supp. 2d 1154 (S.D. Ind. Feb. 5, 2003), James J. Schneider—a licensed CPA and attorney who owned and served as president and "executive reviewer" of Schneider & Company, Inc.—signed a client's (attorney William Conour's) 1992 tax return on October 14, 1993. The return claimed a $49,767 "office expense" deduction representing 50 percent of $99,530 spent on original fine artwork by Indiana artists (including paintings by Otto Stark and T.C. Steele), despite Revenue Ruling 68-232 and 26 U.S.C. § 262 barring depreciation or expensing of fine art and without verifying whether the art was actually given as in-kind employee compensation. When the IRS assessed a preparer penalty under 26 U.S.C. § 6694(b)(2), Schneider sought to escape liability by arguing that his employee CPA (Brian D. Rhea) had performed the underlying work and prepared the "substantial portion" of the return. Judge Tinder rejected Schneider's reliance on Goulding and granted summary judgment to the United States. The court held that under the disjunctive definition of 26 U.S.C. § 7701(a)(36)(A) ("any person who prepares for compensation, or who employs one or more persons to prepare for compensation") and 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(b)(2), an employer/owner who signs a tax return is, as a matter of law, a signing tax return preparer and cannot escape § 6694 liability or his duty of reasonable inquiry by shifting blame onto staff who performed the underlying calculations.
3.4 Tiddy v. United States, 762 F. Supp. 122 (W.D.N.C. 1991)

In Tiddy v. United States, 762 F. Supp. 122 (W.D.N.C. Mar. 28, 1991), the court examined what constitutes preparing a return "for compensation" under 26 U.S.C. § 7701(a)(36)(A) and 26 CFR § 301.7701-15. The plaintiff, Junius A. Tiddy, and two employees in his real estate and furniture business prepared approximately 360 Forms 1040A and 1040EZ in 1984 and 600 returns in 1985 for individuals from whom Tiddy purchased tax refund claims at a discount, without charging any separate or explicit fee labeled "tax return preparation". While the court barred retroactive enforcement of roughly $300,000 in IRC § 6695(c) and (f) penalties prior to Revenue Ruling 86-55 because Tiddy's returns contained zero errors, Judge McMillan held as a matter of law that part of the profit realized from discounting the refunds constituted compensation for preparing the returns, declaring Tiddy a paid tax return preparer under 26 U.S.C. § 7701(a)(36)(A) prospectively. Under Tiddy and 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(f)(1)(xii), a boutique R&D firm that bundles "free" Form 6765 preparation into an engineering consulting fee, software platform subscription, or contingent percentage of tax savings is unequivocally preparing a portion of the return "for compensation".
4. PTIN Registration vs. Return Disclosure: Resolving the Regulatory Divergence
4.1 Two Different Standards (Substantial Portion vs. All or Substantially All)

A critical technical nuance in U.S. tax administration—and a frequent source of confusion for boutique R&D advisors—is that Treasury regulations employ two different quantitative standards for (1) defining a "tax return preparer" generally under 26 CFR § 301.7701-15 (which governs IRC § 6694 understatement penalties), and (2) defining who must apply for and maintain a Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN) under 26 U.S.C. § 6109(a)(4) and 26 CFR § 1.6109-2 (promulgated by T.D. 9501, 2010-46 I.R.B.).

For general preparer status and IRC § 6694 penalty purposes, 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(a) and (b)(3) apply the "all or a substantial portion" standard, which is triggered whenever a nonsigning advisor prepares a schedule or renders post-event advice on an entry that breaches the $10,000 or $400,000 / 20 percent safe harbor. By contrast, for PTIN disclosure on the filed return under 26 CFR § 1.6109-2(a)(1)–(3) (applicable to returns and claims for refund filed after December 31, 2010), every filed return or claim for refund prepared by one or more tax return preparers must include on the return only the PTIN of the individual signing tax return preparer required by § 1.6695-1(b) to sign the return, together with the EIN of the firm employing or associated with that signing preparer. Nonsigning preparers never enter their PTIN or firm EIN on a return signed by another preparer.
4.2 Practitioner Analysis: Reconciling 26 CFR § 1.6109-2(g) Example 4, IRS PTIN Scenario 7, and IRS PTIN Scenario 10

For purposes of determining who must register with the IRS to obtain and annually renew a PTIN under 26 CFR § 1.6109-2(d), (e), and (f), 26 CFR § 1.6109-2(g) defines a tax return preparer more narrowly as "any individual who is compensated for preparing, or assisting in the preparation of, all or substantially all of a tax return or claim for refund." In evaluating whether an individual has prepared or assisted in preparing "all or substantially all" of a return or refund claim under § 1.6109-2(g), the regulation examines three factors: (1) the complexity of the work performed relative to the overall complexity of the tax return or claim for refund; (2) the amount of the items of income, deductions, or losses attributable to the work performed relative to the total amount of income, deductions, or losses required to be reported on the tax return or claim for refund; and (3) the amount of tax or credit attributable to the work performed relative to the total tax liability required to be shown on the return or claim for refund.

To see how this standard applies to a boutique R&D specialist across original returns, payroll tax filings, and refund claims, practitioners must distinguish three specific authorities in 26 CFR § 1.6109-2(g) and the IRS's official Frequently Asked Questions: Do I Need a PTIN? (updated October 9, 2026):

items: Original Corporate Return Credit Specialist (26 CFR § 1.6109-2(g) Example 4): In Example 4 of 26 CFR § 1.6109-2(g) (and T.D. 9501), Employee E prepares a corporate Form 1120 and consults subject matter expert F regarding a specific tax credit; Expert F calculates the credit amount, which Employee E enters on the Form 1120 alongside the corporation's other income, deductions, and credits. Because the specific tax credit is one of many items on the Form 1120 and does not constitute "all or substantially all" of the overall corporate return, the regulation holds that subject matter expert F is not required to obtain a PTIN, whereas Employee E is required to obtain a PTIN.

Non-Signing Refund Claim Issue Advisor (IRS PTIN Scenario 10): In PTIN Scenario 10 of Frequently Asked Questions: Do I Need a PTIN? (updated October 9, 2026), the IRS directly addresses whether an attorney or CPA must obtain a PTIN if they only advise a client regarding an issue that is reflected on a claim for refund. The IRS states that under the administrative exception authority of 26 CFR § 1.6109-2(h), an attorney or CPA is not required to obtain a PTIN if they only advise a client regarding an issue reflected on a claim for refund and neither they nor any person in their firm signs or is required to sign the claim for refund under 26 CFR §§ 301.7701-15(b)(1) and 1.6695-1(b). Crucially, Scenario 10 explicitly warns that the specialist "is still a non-signing tax return preparer subject to penalty under section 6694 if the attorney or certified public accountant has prepared all or a substantial portion of the claim for refund within the meaning of Treasury Regulation section 301.7701-15(b)(3)."

Payroll Tax Reporting Agent on Forms 94X (IRS PTIN Scenario 7): In PTIN Scenario 7 of the same IRS FAQ guidance, the IRS addresses a reporting agent who prepares Forms 94X series employment tax returns (such as Form 941, to which a QSB's Form 8974 R&D payroll tax credit is attached) for compensation without exercising any discretion or independent judgment regarding the client's underlying tax positions and without rendering tax advice. Because 26 CFR § 1.6109-2(g) incorporates the mechanical assistance carve-out of 26 CFR § 301.7701-15(f) and Example 1 of § 301.7701-15(f)(6), the reporting agent in Scenario 7 is not a tax return preparer and does not need a PTIN. Conversely, if a boutique R&D advisor prepares all or substantially all of a standalone Form 1120-X or Form 941-X refund claim (or if a non-signing employee at the boutique firm prepares all or substantially all of that standalone refund claim for a signing partner to review and sign, as in 26 CFR § 1.6109-2(g) Example 3 and PTIN Scenario 13), both the non-signing associate and the signing principal must hold active PTINs.

5. Penalty Exposure and Cross-Firm Liability Allocation (IRC §§ 6694, 6695, and 6701)
5.1 The Statutory vs. Regulatory Conflict on IRC § 6694(b) and Current Penalty Rates

When an IRS examination disallows all or part of an IRC § 41 research credit claim, the Internal Revenue Code provides four distinct civil and criminal penalty regimes targeting preparers and advisors—plus a critical conflict between the current statutory text of 26 U.S.C. § 6694(b) and the unamended text of 26 CFR §§ 1.6694-1(a)(1) and 1.6694-3(a)(1) that practitioners must recognize.

First, 26 U.S.C. § 6694(a) (as amended by Pub. L. 110-343 in 2008) and 26 CFR §§ 1.6694-1 and 1.6694-2 (Understatement Due to Unreasonable Positions) impose a penalty equal to the greater of $1,000 or 50 percent of the income derived (or to be derived) by the tax return preparer with respect to the return or claim for refund. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6694(a)(1)–(2) and Revenue Procedure 2009-11 (2009-3 I.R.B.), this penalty applies to any signing or nonsigning tax return preparer who prepares a covered return or claim for refund (or a substantial portion thereof) with respect to which any part of an understatement of tax liability is due to a position of which the preparer knew (or reasonably should have known), unless: (A) for an undisclosed position (other than a tax shelter or reportable transaction), there is or was substantial authority for the position (defined under 26 CFR § 1.6662-4(d)); (B) for a position adequately disclosed in accordance with 26 CFR § 1.6694-2(d)(3) (other than a tax shelter or reportable transaction), there is a reasonable basis for the position (defined under 26 CFR § 1.6662-3(b)(3)); or (C) for a tax shelter (as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 6662(d)(2)(C)(ii)) or a reportable transaction to which 26 U.S.C. § 6662A applies, it is reasonable to believe that the position would more likely than not (a greater than 50 percent likelihood per Notice 2009-5 and IRM 20.1.6) be sustained on its merits. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6694(a)(3) and 26 CFR § 1.6694-2(e), no penalty is imposed under § 6694(a) if it is shown that there is reasonable cause for the understatement and the tax return preparer acted in good faith. Under 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(a)(2), for a signing preparer, the return is deemed prepared on the date it is signed (or the date filed if the signing preparer fails to sign); for a nonsigning boutique R&D advisor, the relevant date is the date the nonsigning preparer provides the tax advice with respect to the position giving rise to the understatement, determined based on all facts and circumstances.

Second, 26 U.S.C. § 6694(b) (Understatement Due to Willful or Reckless Conduct) applies where any part of an understatement of liability is due to (A) a willful attempt in any manner to understate the liability for tax on the return or claim, or (B) a reckless or intentional disregard of rules or regulations (which include the provisions of the Internal Revenue Code, temporary or final Treasury regulations issued under the Code, and revenue rulings or notices—other than notices of proposed rulemaking—published in the Internal Revenue Bulletin per 26 CFR § 1.6694-3(e)). Here, practitioners must account for a direct conflict between the unamended 2008 Treasury regulations and the enacted federal statute:

items: Unamended Treasury Regulations (26 CFR § 1.6694-1(a)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.6694-3(a)(1), promulgated by T.D. 9436 on Dec. 22, 2008, applicable after Dec. 31, 2008): State that the § 6694(b) penalty is equal to "the greater of $5,000 or 50 percent of the income derived (or to be derived) by the tax return preparer."

Enacted Statute (26 U.S.C. § 6694(b)(1)(B), as amended by Section 210(a) of the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes [PATH] Act of 2015, Division Q of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2016, Pub. L. 114-113, 129 Stat. 3085, enacted Dec. 18, 2015), IRM 20.1.6 (updated Aug. 10, 2026), and Official IRS Guidance (irs.gov/payments/tax-preparer-penalties, updated Sept. 21, 2026): Explicitly amended 26 U.S.C. § 6694(b)(1)(B) by substituting "75 percent" for "50 percent", effective for returns prepared for taxable years ending after December 18, 2015.

Legal Weight Resolution: Because a federal statute enacted by Congress carries superior legal authority over an unamended Treasury regulation that recites prior statutory text, the controlling legal penalty under 26 U.S.C. § 6694(b)(1) for all current tax years is the greater of $5,000 or 75 percent of the income derived (or to be derived) by the tax return preparer. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6694(b)(3) and IRM 20.1.6, any penalty payable under § 6694(b) is reduced by the amount of any penalty paid under § 6694(a) for the same return or claim, so that the combined assessment under §§ 6694(a) and (b) cannot exceed the greater of $5,000 or 75 percent of the income derived. Furthermore, under IRM 20.1.6, IRS examiners calculating an IRC § 6694(b) penalty using the percentage-of-income method must elevate the calculation determination through their manager to the functional Return Preparer Coordinator (RPC), who consults with local IRS Counsel, and must secure timely written managerial approval under 26 U.S.C. § 6751(b)(1).
