5.2 Analysis: Cross-Firm Liability Allocation (26 CFR § 1.6694-1(b))

How does the IRS allocate IRC § 6694 liability when a corporate taxpayer's return is signed by Partner A at CPA Firm X, but the disallowed Form 6765 R&D tax credit was calculated by Advisor D at Boutique R&D Firm Y? Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(b)(1)–(6) establishes a sharp structural divide between intra-firm allocation and inter-firm allocation.

Within any single firm (26 CFR § 1.6694-1(b)(1)–(4)), "there is only one individual within a firm who is primarily responsible for each position on the return or claim for refund giving rise to an understatement." If a preparer within that firm signs the return, the signing preparer is presumptively considered the individual within the firm who is primarily responsible for all positions on the return giving rise to an understatement, unless credible information from any source establishes that the signing preparer is not primarily responsible and that a nonsigning preparer within that same firm had primary responsibility (§ 1.6694-1(b)(2) and (b)(6) Examples 1 and 2). Even if credible evidence supports a finding that both the signing preparer and a nonsigning specialist within the same firm are responsible, the IRS may assess the § 6694 penalty against either one of the individuals within that firm, but not both (§ 1.6694-1(b)(4) and (b)(6) Example 5). If no one in the firm signed the return—which is always the case for an external boutique R&D firm on an original return signed by an outside CPA or self-prepared by the taxpayer—then under 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(b)(3), the nonsigning tax return preparer within the boutique firm who has overall supervisory responsibility for the position giving rise to the understatement is deemed the primarily responsible preparer within that boutique firm, unless credible information establishes that another nonsigning preparer within the boutique firm is primarily responsible (§ 1.6694-1(b)(6) Example 3).

By contrast, when the signing CPA and the nonsigning boutique R&D advisor are employed by or associated with different firms (26 CFR § 1.6694-1(b)(1) and (b)(6) Example 4), the single-individual limit does not apply across the two separate firms:

"In the course of identifying the individual who is primarily responsible for the position, the IRS may advise multiple individuals within the firm that it may be concluded that they are the individual within the firm who is primarily responsible. In some circumstances, there may be more than one tax return preparer who is primarily responsible for the position(s) giving rise to an understatement if multiple tax return preparers are employed by, or associated with, different firms."

In 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(b)(6) Example 4, Attorney A signs Client C's tax return, relying on advice regarding a substantial position provided by Attorney D, who works for a different firm than A; the regulation holds that D may also be concluded to be primarily responsible for the position and subject to penalty under section 6694 alongside A's firm.

In addition to the individual supervisory advisor at the boutique firm, the boutique R&D firm entity itself is subject to a separate entity-level § 6694 penalty under 26 CFR §§ 1.6694-1(b)(5), 1.6694-2(a)(2), and 1.6694-3(a)(2) (as well as IRM 20.1.6) if, and only if: (i) one or more members of the principal management (or principal officers) of the firm or a branch office participated in or knew of the proscribed conduct; (ii) the corporation, partnership, or other firm entity failed to provide reasonable and appropriate procedures for review of the position for which the penalty is imposed; or (iii) the firm entity disregarded its reasonable and appropriate review procedures through willfulness, recklessness, or gross indifference (including ignoring facts that would lead a person of reasonable prudence and competence to investigate or ascertain) in formulating the advice or preparing the return or claim for refund. Under 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(f)(3)–(4) Example 3, when both an individual employee and their employing firm are penalized, the individual employee's penalty is capped at 50 percent (or 75 percent under § 6694(b)) of the portion of the individual's compensation allocable to the hours spent on that position, and the firm's entity-level penalty equals 50 percent (or 75 percent) of the total fee earned by the firm for that position, reduced by the dollar penalty assessed against the individual employee.
5.3 Worked Hypothetical Example: Computing Fee Allocation and Multi-Party Penalties (26 CFR § 1.6694-1(f))

To see how 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(f) ("Income derived (or to be derived) with respect to the return or claim for refund") operates in an audit of a boutique R&D credit study, consider a hypothetical case modeled directly on 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(f)(4) Examples 1 through 3. Suppose Corporate Taxpayer Delta Corp engages Boutique R&D Firm Y under a $50,000 lump-sum contract. Of that $50,000, a reasonable time-and-deliverable allocation shows that $5,000 was paid for prospective documentation and project-tracking consulting rendered before the research events occurred, while $45,000 was paid for the post-year-end Research Credit Study and Form 6765 calculations (which reported $600,000 in QREs and a $63,000.00 gross research credit). Within Boutique R&D Firm Y, Senior Manager M (who is a salaried employee and not an equity partner) had overall supervisory responsibility for Delta's R&D study; M earns an annual salary of $75,000, billed 2,000 total hours during the year, and spent 100 hours on Delta's post-event R&D study. Additionally, Boutique R&D Firm Y's managing principal participated in approving the study methodology, which lacked substantial authority and was not disclosed. Delta Corp's general accounting firm, CPA Firm X, charged Delta $12,000 to prepare and sign Delta's Form 1120.
Applying the step-by-step rules of 26 U.S.C. § 6694 and 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(f) yields the following exact figures:

items: Allocation of Pre-Event vs. Post-Event Compensation (26 CFR § 1.6694-1(f)(2)(ii) & (f)(4) Example 1): Compensation for advice rendered prior to the events occurring ($5,000) is excluded from "income derived" unless tainted by an anti-avoidance scheme under § 301.7701-15(b)(2)(i). Thus, the post-event income derived by Boutique R&D Firm Y with respect to the Form 6765 position is 50,000 − $5,000 = $45,000.00).

Total Penalty Exposure under IRC § 6694(a) (Unreasonable Position — 50% Rate): The total § 6694(a) penalty is the greater of $1,000 or 50 percent of $45,000, which equals $22,500.00 (0.50 × $45,000 = $22,500.00). Under 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(f)(4) Example 3, Supervisory Manager M's allocated compensation for the position is $3,750.00 ((100 hours ÷ 2,000 hours) × $75,000 = $3,750.00), so M's individual 50 percent penalty is capped at $1,875.00 (0.50 × $3,750.00 = $1,875.00), and Boutique R&D Firm Y's entity-level penalty is reduced by M's assessment to 22,500.00 − $1,875.00 = $20,625.00).

Total Penalty Exposure under IRC § 6694(b) (Willful or Reckless Disregard of IRC § 41 Rules — 75% Statutory Rate per 26 U.S.C. § 6694(b)(1)(B)): Under the controlling 75 percent statutory rate enacted by Pub. L. 114-113, the total § 6694(b) penalty is the greater of $5,000 or 75 percent of $45,000, which equals $33,750.00 (0.75 × $45,000 = $33,750.00)—allocated as $2,812.50 against Manager M (0.75 × $3,750.00 = $2,812.50) and 33,750.00 − $2,812.50 = $30,937.50). (Under the superseded 50 percent rate still printed in unamended 26 CFR § 1.6694-3(a)(1), the total figure would have been $22,500.00, a difference of $11,250.00.)

15 Percent Partial Payment to Stay Collection Pending Refund Litigation (26 U.S.C. § 6694(c)(1)–(3), IRM 20.1.6, and 26 CFR § 1.6696-1(e)): Under 26 U.S.C. § 6694(c)(1) and IRM 20.1.6, if the IRS issues a statement of notice and demand for the penalty under 26 CFR § 1.6696-1(a), Boutique R&D Firm Y and Manager M may stay IRS levy and court collection proceedings (and suspend the IRC § 6502 collection statute of limitations under § 6694(c)(3)) by paying at least 15 percent of the assessed penalty within 30 days after the day of notice and demand and filing a separate claim for refund under penalty of perjury on Form 6118 (Claim for Refund of Tax Return Preparer and Promoter Penalties, prescribed by 26 CFR § 1.6696-1(b)–(e)), followed by filing a district court refund suit within 30 days after denial of the Form 6118 claim (or, if earlier, within 30 days after the expiration of 6 months from filing the claim) under 26 U.S.C. § 6694(c)(2). The required 15 percent deposit equals $3,375.00 for the § 6694(a) penalty (0.15 × $22,500.00 = $3,375.00) or $5,062.50 for the § 6694(b) penalty (0.15 × $33,750.00 = $5,062.50). Moreover, under 26 U.S.C. § 6694(d), if a final administrative determination or judicial decision later establishes that there was no understatement of Delta Corp's tax liability, any § 6694 assessment must be automatically abated and refunded without regard to any period of limitations.

CPA Firm X's Separate Liability Evaluation (26 CFR §§ 1.6694-1(e)(1), (e)(3) Example 3, and 1.6694-2(e)(5)): Under 26 CFR § 1.6694-2(e)(5) and § 1.6694-1(e)(1), the signing partner at CPA Firm X may rely in good faith without independent verification on schedules or advice prepared by another advisor (Boutique R&D Firm Y) whom the CPA had reason to believe was competent, and is not required to independently audit or examine books and records, unless (i) the advice or schedule is unreasonable on its face, (ii) the CPA knew or should have known that the boutique advisor was not aware of all relevant facts, or (iii) the CPA knew or should have known (given the nature of the CPA's practice) that the advice was no longer reliable due to developments in the law since it was given. If the signing CPA satisfies this good-faith reasonable inquiry standard (analogous to Accountant G relying on an enrolled actuary's IRC § 404 pension limit calculation in 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(e)(3) Example 3), CPA Firm X owes $0 in penalties, while Boutique R&D Firm Y and Manager M bear the entire $22,500.00 (or $33,750.00) penalty. Conversely, if the boutique study was facially unreasonable (for example, claiming 100 percent of executive officer wages without time tracking or claiming post-production routine quality control excluded by 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A)) and the signing CPA ignored those red flags in violation of 26 CFR § 1.6694-1(e)(1), CPA Firm X can also be assessed a separate § 6694(a) penalty of $6,000.00 (0.50 × $12,000 = $6,000.00).

body.text: 6. How a Nonsigning Boutique R&D Advisor Protects Itself: Adequate Disclosure Without a Signature (26 CFR § 1.6694-2(d)(3)(ii))
6.1 The Two-Track Nonsigning Disclosure Regime

A central practical question arises for boutique R&D advisors: If a boutique R&D advisor does not sign the tax return and does not control the physical or electronic filing transmission of the return, how can the boutique advisor protect itself from an IRC § 6694(a) penalty (or an IRC § 6694(b) reckless/intentional disregard penalty under 26 CFR § 1.6694-3(c)(2)) when an R&D tax credit position has a "reasonable basis" (defined under 26 CFR §§ 1.6662-3(b)(3) and 1.6694-2(d)(2)) but might be challenged by an IRS engineer as lacking "substantial authority"?

A signing preparer must either (A) disclose the position in accordance with 26 CFR § 1.6662-4(f) on a properly completed Form 8275 (Disclosure Statement) or Form 8275-R (Regulation Disclosure Statement) attached to the filed return (or on the return pursuant to the annual revenue procedure under § 1.6662-4(f)(2)), (B) provide the taxpayer with the prepared tax return containing the Form 8275/8275-R disclosure statement (as illustrated by Accountant R in 26 CFR § 1.6694-2(d)(3)(v) Example 1), or (C) for returns subject to section 6662 penalties other than the substantial understatement penalty under § 6662(b)(2) and (d), advise the taxpayer of the penalty standards under section 6662 and contemporaneously document that advice in the preparer's files (26 CFR § 1.6694-2(d)(3)(i)(A)–(C)). Because a nonsigning tax return preparer cannot force a taxpayer or an external CPA firm to attach Form 8275 to the final return, 26 CFR § 1.6694-2(d)(3)(ii) provides a dedicated safe harbor tailored specifically for nonsigning preparers.

Under 26 CFR § 1.6694-2(d)(3)(ii) (for positions other than tax shelters or IRC § 6662A reportable transactions that satisfy the reasonable basis standard), if the position is not disclosed on Form 8275 with the return, a nonsigning boutique R&D advisor nevertheless achieves adequate disclosure—immunizing the boutique advisor from § 6694(a) penalties even if no Form 8275 is ever filed with the IRS—by satisfying either of two communication and contemporaneous documentation rules depending on the recipient of the study:

items: Track A — Advice Delivered to the Taxpayer (26 CFR § 1.6694-2(d)(3)(ii)(A)): When the nonsigning boutique R&D advisor provides its study and advice directly to the taxpayer, disclosure is adequate if the boutique advisor advises the taxpayer of any opportunity to avoid penalties under section 6662 that could apply to the position, if relevant, and of the standards for disclosure to the extent applicable, and contemporaneously documents the advice in the boutique advisor's files. In 26 CFR § 1.6694-2(d)(3)(v) Example 2, Attorney S advises a large corporate taxpayer on complex return entries constituting a substantial portion of the return, concludes one position lacks substantial authority though it meets the reasonable basis standard, advises the corporate taxpayer that the position lacks substantial authority and that the taxpayer may be subject to an accuracy-related penalty under section 6662 unless the position is disclosed in a disclosure statement included in the return, and contemporaneously documents in S's files that this advice was provided at the time the advice was given; even though neither S nor anyone in S's firm signs the return and the corporate taxpayer files without disclosing, S is not subject to a penalty under section 6694.

Track B — Advice Delivered to Another Tax Return Preparer (26 CFR § 1.6694-2(d)(3)(ii)(B)): When the nonsigning boutique R&D advisor provides its advice or schedules to another tax return preparer outside the boutique firm (such as the client's external signing CPA firm), disclosure is adequate if the boutique advisor advises the other tax return preparer that disclosure under section 6694(a) may be required, and contemporaneously documents that advice in the boutique advisor's files confirming that the preparer outside the firm was so advised.

body.text: 6.2 Practitioner Analysis: Structuring Contemporaneous Penalty and Disclosure Memoranda

To invoke Track A or Track B successfully during an IRS examination, boutique R&D firms must strictly comply with 26 CFR § 1.6694-2(d)(3)(iii) (Requirements for advice). That regulation establishes an absolute prohibition against boilerplate disclaimers:

"A general disclaimer will not satisfy the requirement that the tax return preparer provide and contemporaneously document advice regarding the likelihood that a position will be sustained on the merits and the potential application of penalties as a result of that position."

While 26 CFR § 1.6694-2(d)(3)(iii) permits a boutique R&D firm to use established forms or templates to explain the general operation of the IRC §§ 6662 and 6694 penalty and Form 8275 disclosure provisions, every specific return position in the R&D study for which there is a reasonable basis but not substantial authority (for example, a contested Dual Function Software [DFS] subset or Internal Use Software [IUS] High-Threshold-of-Innovation position reported in Section G, Line 49(e) of Form 6765) must be explicitly identified and addressed, and the written advice must be particular to the taxpayer, tailored to the taxpayer's specific facts and circumstances, and saved in the boutique firm's permanent engagement file at the time the Form 6765 deliverable is transmitted to the client and the signing CPA. Furthermore, if the boutique advisor's study is intended to help the taxpayer establish a reasonable-cause and good-faith defense against taxpayer accuracy-related penalties under 26 U.S.C. § 6662 (or the 20 percent erroneous refund claim penalty under 26 U.S.C. § 6676), the study must also satisfy the three minimum standards of 26 CFR § 1.6664-4(c)(1): (i) the advice must be based upon all pertinent facts and circumstances and the law as it relates to them; (ii) the advice must not be based on unreasonable factual or legal assumptions or unreasonably rely on taxpayer representations, statements, findings, or projections known to be unlikely to be true; and (iii) if challenging a regulation's validity, the position must be adequately disclosed on Form 8275-R.
7. Operational, Ethical, and Audit Compliance Workflow for Boutique R&D Engagements
7.1 IRS Examination of Boutique R&D Studies, Engagement Letters, and Reportable Transactions

Under the IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG, Credit for Increasing Research Activities IRC § 41, May 2008) and IRS News Releases IR-2017-27 (Excessive Claims for Business Credits Makes the IRS "Dirty Dozen" List of Tax Scams, Feb. 9, 2017) and IR-2016-29 (IRS Wraps Up the "Dirty Dozen" List of Tax Scams for 2016, Feb. 19, 2016), IRS examiners and Research Credit Technical Advisors (RCTAs) scrutinize prepackaged, multi-binder Research Credit Studies prepared by third-party boutique consultants across three standard phases: Phase 1 (Initial Evaluation / Feasibility Assessment to determine whether the taxpayer is entitled to a credit or additional credit and develop a study plan), Phase 2 (Execution of Study Plan — reviewing accounting records, conducting employee interviews, questionnaires, and physical inspections), and Phase 3 (Compilation of Findings — producing the Summary Report, Methodology Report, Departmental/Project Reports, QRE spreadsheets, and Form 6765 / refund claim schedules).

Mandatory IDR and Summons for the Boutique Advisor's Engagement Letter: The RCCATG instructs IRS field examiners to issue an Information Document Request (IDR) simultaneously with the mandatory Research Credit Claim IDR—and, if the taxpayer refuses to produce it, to consider issuing an administrative summons with the assistance of local IRS Counsel—demanding a copy of the engagement letter and any supplemental contracts between the taxpayer and the outside R&D consultant (explicitly noting that consultant engagement letters are not privileged). IRS examiners review the boutique R&D advisor's engagement letter for three specific enforcement triggers:

items: Methodology and Scope Audit: Identifying the details of each phase of the study, the specific names of the boutique consultant's employees who conducted the study and their assigned tasks, whether and how taxpayer employee interviews were conducted, the list of records requested from the taxpayer, the specific work products created, whether base-year consistency rules under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(5) (and Form 6765 Section E, Line 40 regarding new or recharacterized expense categories) were properly analyzed, and whether unsupported estimates were used without a factual basis.

Reportable Transaction Triggers (26 CFR § 1.6011-4 and IRC § 6707A): Determining whether the boutique advisor's fee structure or confidentiality clauses turned the R&D study into a Reportable Transaction requiring the taxpayer to file Form 8886 (Reportable Transaction Disclosure Statement) under 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(d). Specifically, examiners screen the engagement letter for Confidential Transactions under 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(3) (where the advisor imposes conditions of confidentiality on the taxpayer's disclosure of the tax treatment or structure of the study for a minimum fee) and Transactions with Contractual Protection under 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(4) (where the taxpayer has the right to a full or partial refund of fees if all or part of the intended tax consequences from the R&D credit claim are not sustained, or where fees are contingent on the taxpayer's realization of tax benefits from the transaction, subject to applicable IRS revenue procedure carve-outs). If a transaction is a reportable transaction to which IRC § 6662A applies, the preparer penalty standard under 26 U.S.C. § 6694(a)(2)(C) escalates from "substantial authority" to "more likely than not" (greater than 50 percent likelihood), and failure by the taxpayer to attach Form 8886 triggers strict-liability penalties under 26 U.S.C. § 6707A.
Shift of Resolution Control: The RCCATG specifically flags boutique fee agreements that shift ultimate control over the audit resolution of the claim from the taxpayer to the third-party preparer.

body.text: 7.2 Circular 230 Contingent Fee Restrictions (31 CFR § 10.27) and Ridgely v. Lew

Because many boutique R&D advisors price their studies as a contingent percentage of the research credit calculated on Form 6765, practitioners must navigate Treasury Department Circular 230 (31 CFR Part 10, Subpart B) and federal judicial limits on IRS fee regulation.

Under 31 CFR § 10.27(b)–(c) (promulgated by T.D. 9359, 72 FR 54548, Sept. 26, 2007, applicable to fee arrangements entered into after March 26, 2008), a "contingent fee" is defined broadly to include any fee that is based, in whole or in part, on whether or not a position taken on a tax return or other filing avoids challenge by the IRS or is sustained either by the IRS or in litigation, including any fee based on a percentage of the refund reported on a return, any fee based on a percentage of the taxes saved, or any fee arrangement in which the practitioner will reimburse the client for all or a portion of the fee if the position is challenged or not sustained (whether via an indemnity agreement, guarantee, or rescission right). Textually, § 10.27(b)(1)–(4) prohibits practitioners from charging a contingent fee for services rendered in connection with any matter before the IRS—except for: (i) services rendered in connection with the IRS's examination of, or challenge to, an original tax return (§ 10.27(b)(2)(i)); (ii) services rendered in connection with an amended return or claim for refund or credit where the amended return or claim was filed within 120 days of the taxpayer receiving a written notice of the examination of, or a written challenge to, the original tax return (§ 10.27(b)(2)(ii)); (iii) services rendered in connection with a claim for credit or refund filed solely in connection with the determination of statutory interest or penalties assessed by the IRS (§ 10.27(b)(3)); or (iv) services rendered in connection with any judicial proceeding arising under the Internal Revenue Code (§ 10.27(b)(4)).

However, in Ridgely v. Lew, Civil Action No. 1:12-cv-00565 (CRC), 55 F. Supp. 3d 89 (D.D.C. July 16, 2014), practicing CPA Gerald Lee Ridgely, Jr. sued the Secretary of the Treasury and the Commissioner of the IRS under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. §§ 701–706) to challenge 31 CFR § 10.27's prohibition on charging contingent fees for preparing and filing Ordinary Refund Claims—defined by the court as refund claims filed after a taxpayer has submitted an original tax return, but before the IRS has initiated an audit/examination of that return and prior to any formal legal representation or adversarial proceeding. Applying Chevron Step 1 and the D.C. Circuit's precedent in Loving v. IRS, 742 F.3d 1013 (D.C. Cir. 2014), United States District Judge Christopher Reid Cooper held that 31 U.S.C. § 330(a)(1)—which authorizes the Treasury Secretary to "regulate the practice of representatives of persons before the Department of the Treasury"—does not grant the IRS statutory authority to regulate the preparation and filing of tax returns or Ordinary Refund Claims prior to the commencement of an adversarial IRS audit or formal representation. The court held 31 CFR § 10.27(a) and (b) invalid to the extent they prohibit contingent fees for preparing and filing Ordinary Refund Claims prior to an audit, granted summary judgment to Ridgely, and entered a permanent injunction barring the IRS from enforcing § 10.27 against Ordinary Refund Claims. (Practitioners who are CPAs must nevertheless also comply with state board of accountancy rules and the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct Rule 1.510.010 on contingent fees.)
Three additional Circular 230 provisions directly govern practitioners who prepare or rely upon boutique R&D studies:

items: 31 CFR § 10.22 (Diligence as to Accuracy, paragraph (a) effective Sept. 26, 2007; paragraph (b) effective June 12, 2014): Requires due diligence in preparing or assisting in the preparation of, approving, and filing tax returns, documents, affidavits, and other papers relating to IRS matters. Under § 10.22(b), a signing CPA relying on a boutique R&D advisor's work product is presumed to have exercised due diligence only if the practitioner used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating the specialist, taking proper account of the nature of the relationship between the practitioner and the specialist.

31 CFR § 10.34 (Standards with Respect to Tax Returns and Documents, Affidavits and Other Papers, paragraph (a) effective Aug. 2, 2011; paragraphs (b)–(d) effective Sept. 26, 2007): Explicitly governs both signing preparers (§ 10.34(a)(1)(i)) and nonsigning specialists (§ 10.34(a)(1)(ii)) who "[a]dvise a client to take a position on a tax return or claim for refund, or prepare a portion of a tax return or claim for refund containing a position"—prohibiting positions that lack a reasonable basis or violate IRC § 6694(a)(2) or (b)(2), and requiring the practitioner under § 10.34(c)(1)–(3) to inform the client of potential penalties and disclosure opportunities even if the practitioner is not personally subject to a penalty under the Internal Revenue Code with respect to the position.

31 CFR § 10.37 (Requirements for Written Advice, T.D. 9668, 79 FR 33693, effective for written advice rendered after June 12, 2014): Mandates that written tax advice (such as a formal R&D Tax Credit Study deliverable) must (i) be based on reasonable factual and legal assumptions, (ii) reasonably consider all relevant facts and circumstances that the practitioner knows or reasonably should know, (iii) use reasonable efforts to identify and ascertain the facts relevant to written advice on each federal tax matter, (iv) not rely upon representations, statements, findings, or agreements (including projections or forecasts) if reliance would be unreasonable, (v) relate applicable law and authorities to facts, and (vi) never, in evaluating a federal tax matter, take into account the possibility that a tax return will not be audited or that a matter will not be raised on audit (§ 10.37(a)(2)(vi)). Under § 10.37(c)(2), a heightened reasonable-practitioner standard applies where the practitioner knows or has reason to know the opinion will be used by another person in promoting, marketing, or recommending an arrangement with a significant purpose of tax avoidance. (When T.D. 9668 amended § 10.37 effective June 12, 2014, it replaced the older "Covered Opinion" rules under former 31 CFR § 10.35(b)(7) and (e)(4) referenced in the 2008 RCCATG with the unified written advice standard of § 10.37.)

body.text: 7.3 The Amended Return Five Items of Information Rule and Form 6765 Section G (2025–2027)

When a boutique R&D advisor prepares a Research Credit Study, two major substantive reporting mandates—one governing amended returns and refund claims, and one governing the redesigned Form 6765 Sections E, F, and G—directly impact preparer due diligence and signing/nonsigning responsibilities.

First, under the IRS Research Credit Claims (Section 41) on Amended Returns Frequently Asked Questions (and the Instructions for Form 6765), following the expiration of the initial grace period on January 10, 2022 (with the IRS transition period extended through January 10, 2027), any refund claim involving an IRC § 41 research credit is legally valid only if the taxpayer provides five mandatory items of information at the time the refund claim is filed with the IRS (attached electronically as Form6765ClaimInformation.pdf if e-filed):

items: Identify all the business components (as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(B)—any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business) to which the IRC § 41 research credit claim relates for that claim year;

For each business component, identify all research activities performed (demonstrating satisfaction of the four-part test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)–(6): the Section 174A domestic research expenditure test, the technological information test, the business component test, and the process of experimentation test where at least 80 percent—"substantially all"—of the research activities measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose of new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality);

Name the individuals who performed each research activity (or, per current IRS FAQ guidance, provide the specific number of individuals and each individual's title or position in lieu of specific names);

Identify the information each individual sought to discover (to eliminate technical uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design for developing or improving the business component under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)); and

Provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (which may be done using Form 6765, including statistical samples computed pursuant to Rev. Proc. 2011-42).

body.text: During the transition period running through January 10, 2027, if the IRS determines that a timely filed research credit refund claim is deficient because it is missing any of the five required items, the IRS notifies the taxpayer via Letter 6426C or Letter 6428, which specifies the missing items and grants the taxpayer 45 days from the date on the letter to perfect the claim. The IRS explicitly warns that an original submission or 45-day response that merely repeats the research credit legal definitions and requirements from the Internal Revenue Code or Treasury Regulations is deemed insufficient, and if sufficient information is not received within the 45-day perfection window, the entire claim for refund is rejected. For BBA partnerships, which cannot file amended returns and must instead file an Administrative Adjustment Request (AAR) submitting Forms 8985 and 8986 to the IRS and sending Forms 8986 to their partners, the partnership does not need to repeat the required research credit items on Forms 8985 and 8986 if those items are included with the Form 6765 attached to the partnership's AAR.

Second, under the December 2025 Instructions for Form 6765 (updated April 30, 2026) and the June 18, 2025 controlled-group clarification (updated June 28, 2026), the redesigned Form 6765 adds three detailed reporting sections that typically require a boutique R&D advisor's engineering and accounting input. Section E (Other Information, Lines 37–41) must be completed whenever QREs are reported on Line 48 (for only the filing member's QREs if part of a controlled group), requiring (Line 37) the total number of business components generating the QREs on Line 48, (Line 38) the total amount of corporate officers' wages included on Line 42, (Line 39) whether the taxpayer acquired or disposed of any major portion of a trade or business during the tax year, (Line 40) whether any new or recharacterized categories of expenses were included as current-year QREs compared to base years, and (Line 41) whether the taxpayer determined any QREs following the ASC 730 Directive (available only to taxpayers with assets of $10,000,000 or more that follow U.S. GAAP to prepare Certified Audited Financial Statements showing current R&D expenses and reconcile book-to-tax income on Schedule M-3). Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary, Lines 42–48) summarizes the filing member's total qualified wages (Line 42), supplies (Line 43), rental or lease costs of computers (Line 44), applicable contract research expenses (Line 45), and basic research payments (Line 46), summing to total QREs on Line 48 (which then flows to Section A, Line 5 or Section B, Line 20). Finally, Section G (Business Component Information, Columns 49(a)–(f) and 50–56) captures component-by-component reporting (for the "80%/Top 50" business components, with remaining components aggregated under "Aggregate Business Components", or sampled components under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 labeled with "sample" and accompanied by Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf), including the conducting member's EIN (49(a)), principal business activity code (49(b)), component name/identifier (49(c)), component type (49(d): Product, Process, or All Others), software classification (49(e): Internal Use Software [IUS], Dual Function Software [DFS], Excepted from IUS, or Non-IUS), description of the information sought to be discovered (49(f)), and a breakdown of direct research wages (Line 50), direct supervision wages (Line 51), direct support wages (Line 52), total qualified wages (Line 53), supplies (Line 54), computer rental/lease costs (Line 55), and contract research expenses (Line 56). Section G is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless filing an amended return claim) and becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025, subject to specific Section G guidelines.
7.4 The Overlooked Privacy Trap: IRC §§ 7216 and 6713 Consent Before Sharing Return Data with a Boutique R&D Advisor

Practitioner Analysis — Why a General CPA Cannot Send Tax Returns to a Boutique R&D Firm Without Written Taxpayer Consent: One of the most frequently overlooked compliance rules in CPA–boutique R&D collaborations is 26 U.S.C. § 7216 (imposing a criminal misdemeanor penalty of up to a $1,000 fine and 1 year imprisonment, or both, plus the costs of prosecution, on any preparer who knowingly or recklessly discloses or uses tax return information for any purpose other than preparing a return) and 26 U.S.C. § 6713 (imposing a civil penalty of $250 per unauthorized disclosure or use, up to $10,000 per calendar year—or $1,000 per occurrence up to a $50,000 calendar year maximum if the unauthorized disclosure or use is connected to an identity theft crime, for disclosures or uses made on or after July 1, 2019). Importantly, under 26 CFR § 301.7216-1(b)(2)(i)–(vi), the definition of a "tax return preparer" for IRC §§ 7216 and 6713 privacy purposes is even broader than under IRC § 7701(a)(36), encompassing anyone engaged in the business of preparing or assisting in preparing returns, providing auxiliary services or software, or performing support duties (as illustrated in 26 CFR § 301.7216-1(b)(2)(vi) Example 1, where employees Q, R, S, and T are all preparers under § 7216 even though only R is a preparer under § 7701(a)(36)).

Under 26 CFR § 301.7216-2(d)(1) (Preparer-to-preparer disclosures, applicable to disclosures occurring on or after January 1, 2009), an officer, employee, or member of a tax return preparer (such as the client's general CPA firm) may disclose tax return information to another tax return preparer located in the United States without formal prior taxpayer consent only "so long as the services provided are not substantive determinations or advice affecting the tax liability reported by taxpayers. A substantive determination involves an analysis, interpretation, or application of the law." The regulation explicitly commands:

"Except as provided in paragraph (c) of this section [which applies only to officers, employees, or members of the same firm located in the United States, and requires prior § 301.7216-3 consent before any disclosure to a preparer located outside the United States], a tax return preparer may not disclose tax return information to another tax return preparer for the purpose of the second tax return preparer making substantive determinations without first receiving the taxpayer's consent in accordance with the rules under § 301.7216-3."

Because a boutique R&D tax advisor's entire role—evaluating projects against the four-part test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), classifying employee wages, supplies, and contract research, and computing the Form 6765 credit—constitutes a substantive determination affecting reported tax liability, a general CPA firm cannot legally send a client's prior tax returns, W-2 wage registers, or trial balances to an external boutique R&D advisor (or to any offshore personnel located outside the United States under § 301.7216-2(c)(2)–(3)) unless the CPA firm first obtains a formal, signed IRC § 7216 written consent from the taxpayer in accordance with 26 CFR § 301.7216-3 (or the taxpayer transmits its own records directly to the boutique advisor). Furthermore, if the boutique R&D advisor uses client data to compile statistical benchmarks for internal management or for marketing or advertising its R&D practice under 26 CFR § 301.7216-2(o) (T.D. 9608, effective December 28, 2012), any disclosed statistical compilation must be completely anonymous as to taxpayer identity, must not disclose an aggregate figure containing data from fewer than 10 tax returns, and is strictly prohibited in any marketing or advertising from identifying dollar amounts of refunds, credits, or deductions, or percentages relating thereto, even if averaged, aggregated, or anonymous.

26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(2)(i)–(ii): Defines "nonsigning tax return preparer" as any preparer who is not a signing preparer but prepares all or a substantial portion of a return or claim with respect to events that have occurred at the time advice is rendered; excludes post-event advice representing < 5 percent of aggregate time spent on the position.
T.D. 9436 (applicable after Dec. 31, 2008); includes three-factor anti-avoidance rule for pre-event advice confirmed post-event.

26 CFR § 301.7701-15(b)(3)(ii)(A)–(C): Nonsigning preparer de minimis safe harbor: an entry/schedule is not a substantial portion if the gross income, deduction, or credit-basis amount (QREs) is (1) < $10,000, or (2) < $400,000 and < 20% of gross income (or AGI for individuals). Inapplicable to signing preparers.
T.D. 9436 (applicable after Dec. 31, 2008). Supersedes pre-2009 safe harbor thresholds of $2,000 and $100,000 / 20% cited in Goulding and Mindell.

26 CFR § 301.7701-15(c) & (d): Furnishing sufficient information/advice so return completion is largely mechanical/clerical makes the advisor a tax return preparer even without placing or reviewing entries on the return; educational qualifications or professional status are not required.

Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) & Instructions: Form 6765 is an informational/computational attachment to the primary tax return (Form 1120, 1120-S, 1065, 1040, 1041) and has no independent signature block. Section G (Business Component Information) is optional for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless on an amended return) and required for tax years beginning after 2025.
Form 6765 (Rev. Dec. 2024); Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. Dec. 2025, updated Apr. 30, 2026 & June 28, 2026)
Form 6765 PDF is Rev. Dec. 2024; Instructions (Rev. Dec. 2025) are for use with the Jan. 2025 revision and incorporate Pub. L. 119-21 (IRC § 174A) and June 18, 2025 group QRE clarifications.

26 U.S.C. § 6109(a)(4), 26 CFR § 1.6109-2, & IRS PTIN FAQs: Only the signing preparer's PTIN and firm EIN appear on the filed return. For PTIN registration, § 1.6109-2(g) applies an "all or substantially all" test and Example 4 excludes subject-matter experts calculating a specific tax credit on Form 1120; PTIN Scenario 10 excludes non-signing refund claim issue advisors; PTIN Scenario 7 excludes non-discretionary Form 94X reporting agents.
Clarified exact distinction between 26 CFR § 1.6109-2(g) Example 4, PTIN Scenario 7 (Form 94X reporting agents), and PTIN Scenario 10 (attorneys/CPAs advising on refund claim issues).

26 U.S.C. § 6694(a) & 26 CFR §§ 1.6694-1, 1.6694-2: Imposes a penalty of the greater of $1,000 or 50 percent of income derived for an understatement due to an unreasonable position (lacking substantial authority if undisclosed, reasonable basis if disclosed, or more-likely-than-not for tax shelters/reportable transactions). Cross-firm liability (§ 1.6694-1(b)(1), Example 4) allows penalizing both a signing CPA and an external nonsigning boutique advisor.
Amended by Pub. L. 110-343 (2008); T.D. 9436 regulations applicable after Dec. 31, 2008; IRM 20.1.6 updated Aug. 10, 2026.

26 U.S.C. § 6694(b)(1)(B) vs. 26 CFR § 1.6694-3(a)(1) (Willful/Reckless Penalty Rate Conflict): Statute imposes the greater of $5,000 or 75 percent of income derived (amended by Pub. L. 114-113, § 210(a), Dec. 18, 2015), whereas unamended 2008 regulation 26 CFR §§ 1.6694-1(a)(1) and 1.6694-3(a)(1) still recite 50 percent.
Statute (Pub. L. 114-113, effective for tax years ending after Dec. 18, 2015), IRM 20.1.6 (Aug. 10, 2026), and IRS guidance (Sept. 21, 2026) control at 75% over unamended 2008 CFR text (50%).

26 U.S.C. § 6695(a)–(h) & 26 CFR §§ 1.6060-1, 1.6107-1, 1.6695-1: Failure to sign return (§ 6695(b)), furnish copy (§ 6695(a)), furnish PTIN (§ 6695(c)), or retain copy/list for 3 years (§ 6695(d)) apply only to signing preparers. Statutory base $50 / $25,000 cap is inflation-adjusted to $60 / $31,500 (2025), $65 / $32,500 (2026), $65 / $33,000 (2027), and $65 / $34,500 (Rev. Proc. 2026-35).
Complete § 6695(a)–(g) schedules across 2022–2028, including $665 for § 6695(f)–(g) in Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (§ 4.54) and $690 in Rev. Proc. 2026-35 (§ 3.59).

26 U.S.C. § 41(a), (b), (c)(4), (d), (h) & 26 U.S.C. § 174A: Provides a 20% regular credit (15.8% reduced under § 280C) or an elected ASC equal to 14% of QREs exceeding 50% of 3-year average prior QREs (6% if no QREs in any of the 3 preceding years; multiplied by 79% if reduced under § 280C); contract research included at 65% (75% for qualified research consortia, 100% for eligible energy research); QSB payroll credit capped at $500,000; § 41(d)(1)(A) references domestic R&E expenditures under § 174A (enacted by Pub. L. 119-21).
